item.title: [www.middleeasteye.net] Sex, drugs, Israeli tech and Trump rivalries: Five explosive claims from Kushner-UAE book
item.description:
Sex, drugs, Israeli tech and Trump rivalries: Five explosive claims from Kushner-UAE book

Submitted by MEE staff on Thu, 11/26/2026 - 20:11
Emirati leader blackmailed his brother over gay sex and oversaw medical treatment that led to nerve damage, US author writes in 'Princes and Thieves'
United Arab Emirates President Mohammed bin Zayed Al Nahyan is seen at a ceremony in Paris, France, on 19 July 2022 (AFP)
Off

An explosive new book by veteran journalist Matthew Cole claims Jared Kushner, President Donald Trump’s son-in-law and Middle East envoy, had a deep entanglement with the governments of Saudi Arabia and particularly the UAE, during the first Trump administration.

The book's most explosive claim is that Kushner was given approximately $2bn from the Saudi and Emirati governments, including $750m held at First Abu Dhabi Bank through an Emirati charity, Watani Al Emarat Foundation, ostensibly to support civic programmes in the Emirates, but in reality used for Emirati weapons purchases and covert military operations.

Kushner, who is currently acting as an envoy for Trump in Ukraine and the Middle East, has vociferously denied the claims.

But the New York Times said the allegations against Kushner should be investigated when Democrats take control of Congress in the new year.

The book, Princes and Thieves: Jared Kushner and Mohamed bin Zayed’s Secret Plot to Remake the Middle East, published last month, contains dozens of other juicy nuggets about the Middle East and the wheeling and dealing that takes place in the region. It also provides a window into the culture of the UAE’s ruling Al Nahyan family.

Cole’s sources are anonymous and MEE couldn’t independently verify all the claims but has selected several highlights below. The UAE and Saudi royal families have not commented on the claims made in the book. 

Homosexual blackmail

Cole claims that in the 1990s, UAE President Mohammed bin Zayed Al Nahyan hired two Syrians to film his brother and rival for the throne, former President Khalifa bin Zayed, having gay sex in a hotel room in southern Europe. Mohammed Bin Zayed then had Russian handlers deliver the tape to the brothers’ father - and founder of the UAE - Zayed bin Sultan Al Nahyan, to embarrass Khalifa.

Albania’s revolt: How Rama’s Kushner resort deal became a threat to his leadership
Read More »

Cole wrote that Zayed bin Sultan realised Mohammed was trying to blackmail his brother, but appreciated his “cunning” and was “amused”. Cole says: “Within the Al Nahyan family, Mohamed’s blackmail attempt came to be seen as an early sign of his ambition to rule the UAE."

Khalifa had only one wife and eight children, which was relatively rare for Gulf royals in the 1990s, but has become more common today.

Although Cole’s reporting on Khalifa bin Zayed’s sexual orientation has not been verified elsewhere, there are other reports of homosexuality among Gulf royals being used against them that have appeared in recent books on the Gulf.

Cole says Mohammed bin Zayed was also seen as hostile to former Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Nayef, who was eventually sidelined by Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman.

According to Cole, Mohammed bin Zayed lobbied the US against Mohammed bin Nayef, on the basis of his alleged homosexuality.

In the case of Mohammed bin Nayef, his sexual orientation has been reported in two well-regarded books on the Saudi kingdom: New York Times Journalist Ben Hubbard’s MBS: The Rise to Power of Mohammed bin Salman and Blood and Oil: Mohammed bin Salman's Ruthless Quest for Global Power, by journalists Bradley Hope and Justin Scheck.

Did UAE ruler drug his brother?

Khalifa bin Zayed became president of the UAE in 2004 after his father’s death. Despite his official title, he widely deferred to his brother, Mohammed bin Zayed, who was crown prince of Abu Dhabi, the UAE’s wealthiest emirate.

Epstein files: Bannon accused UAE's MBZ of 'coughing up' paedophile George Nader
Read More »

Khalifa bin Zayed’s decision to take a back seat to his ostensibly junior brother was often framed in the media as a willing decision that was eventually necessitated by a 2014 stroke he suffered.

Instead, Cole claims that he suffered from alcoholism and an “undiagnosed mental illness” long before. He says that when Mohamed bin Zayed was named deputy crown prince of Abu Dhabi in 2003, he was already providing medical treatments to his brother which left him unable to function.

“Khalifa’s medical treatment left him in a stupor, eventually causing nerve damage,” Cole wrote.

Cole suggests that Mohammed bin Zayed saw the treatment as a way to “undermine” his brother, and often forced the treatment on him with the help of an American nurse with whom he had a family connection.

According to the book, Mohammed bin Zayed had a sexual relationship with the nurse’s niece, Lisa, with whom he fathered an illegitimate child raised in Southern California.

Israeli tech inside UAE F-16s

The UAE is Israel’s closest Arab partner. The two were understood to have enjoyed close security ties for decades before the UAE joined the US-backed Abraham Accords in September 2020, making their relationship public.

DP World replaces Sultan Ahmed bin Sulayem amid UAE tycoon's links to Epstein
Read More »

The UAE has moved closer to Israel amid the US-Israeli war on Iran. The two countries are aligned in regional hotspots like Somaliland and Ethiopia as well.

Cole says that Mohammed bin Zayed was an admirer of Israel since at least the 1990s, despite his father’s reluctance to embrace Israel due to his sympathy with the Palestinians.

In 1998, after reading in Aviation Week about a new F-16 that the US had produced with Israeli software, Mohammed bin Zayed lobbied his father to purchase the warplanes. At the time, Mohammed bin Zayed was the UAE Armed Forces chief of staff and negotiated the purchase with the US.

With Mohammed bin Zayed’s backing, the UAE agreed to purchase 80 aircraft and install Israeli software in them. The decision came amid secret Israeli-Emirati discussions hosted by the Clinton Administration aimed at addressing Israel’s concerns that the sale would endanger its Qualitative Military Edge (QME).

Writer tortured to death

The UAE’s decision to move closer to Israel publicly also sparked a crackdown at home. Cole wrote that Emirati poet Habib Al Sayegh was tortured to death in 2019, after writing a column against normalisation with Israel.

Sayegh was an Emirati luminary who even defended the UAE and Saudi Arabia’s blockade against Qatar. He was very much a member of the UAE’s elite, working as an editor at the Al Khaleej newspaper and serving as secretary general of the Arab Writers Union, according to the book.

Sayegh, however, was vocal in elite circles about the UAE’s growing closeness to Israel. Despite warnings to remain silent, in August 2019 he wrote a column titled “Israel Is Our Real Enemy and A Dangerous Project”.

Following publication of the article, Sayegh was abducted from his home by security officers at the orders of Mohammed bin Zayed, Cole writes. He says he was tortured with a pair of pliers used to pull out several of his teeth by one security agent, while another whipped him with a “belt-like strap with a sharp metal piece attached”.

Sayegh was beaten for three days. When he died, one of Mohammed bin Zayed’s closest aides described his body as “almost unrecognizable,” Cole writes.

Sayegh’s dissent stood in the way of a major diplomatic deal that Mohammed bin Zayed was discussing with Kushner and Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman. Saudi Arabia would eventually grow cool on normalisation with Israel, but the agreement was for the Gulf states to recognise the country and sideline the Palestinians.

Jordan was envisioned as hosting the vast majority of three million Palestinians living in the occupied West Bank, thereby reducing the territory’s population by 90 percent. Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu would then recognise a rump Palestinian state, Cole wrote. The state would also be awarded some land in the Negev desert and Jordanian territory.

Jared Kushner-Tom Barrack rivalry

Cole’s book not only offers a window into the lives and ambitions of Gulf rulers, but also into key figures in the Trump administration. While some of the officials are not in government today, many of them remain central officials in the Middle East.

Besides Jared Kushner, the book discusses Tom Barrack at length. Barrack, a Lebanese-American former private equity investor, is currently US ambassador to Turkey and envoy to Iraq and Syria.

Ten things Tom Barrack said in wild interview on Israel, Lebanon and Muslims
Read More »

Barrack came under fire in the first Trump administration for initiating contact between Trump and the rulers of the UAE and Saudi Arabia before he took office. The book discusses those ties at length, but also suggests that Barrack grew frustrated with Kushner’s rise in the administration.

According to Cole, Barrack wanted to create a Marshall Plan - a reference to the post-WWII fund that rebuilt Europe - for the Middle East, funded by Abu Dhabi and Riyadh, to help develop the region.

But Kushner would only permit Barrack to handle the “Egyptian part” of the Middle East. Barrack would later lobby the UAE to tell Kushner that the Gulf state wanted him as Middle East envoy.

“The message to Barrack was clear: Kushner wouldn’t share White House relationships with MBS and MBZ,” Cole wrote, referring to Mohammed bin Salman and Mohammed bin Zayed.

Barrack and Kushner clashed again when Saudi Arabia and the UAE launched a blockade against Qatar in June 2017. At the time, Riyadh and Abu Dhabi were aligned, although they have more recently fallen out over Yemen, the Iran war and the Red Sea.

Despite his business ties with Saudi Arabia and the UAE, Barrack also tried to maintain good ties with Qatar.

According to the book, when the UAE and Saudi Arabia lobbied Kushner to support the blockade, Barrack joined former Secretary of State Rex Tillerson in pressing Trump not to join.

item.title: [www.middleeasteye.net] University of Michigan faculty vote in support of pro-Palestine students facing charges
item.description:
University of Michigan faculty vote in support of pro-Palestine students facing charges

Submitted by MEE staff on Thu, 11/26/2026 - 18:42
The move comes as a dozen former students and staff face federal criminal charges over the 2024 Gaza encampments
Salma Hamamy (centre) holds a Palestinian flag at a pro-Palestinian protest during the University of Michigan's spring commencement ceremony on 4 May 2024 (Nic Antaya/Getty Images/AFP)
Off

Nearly 60 percent of voting faculty members at the University of Michigan have backed a resolution in support of a dozen former students and staff who are now facing federal criminal charges for their participation in the 2024 anti-war encampments for Gaza. 

The move is symbolic but also an indication of where much of the teaching staff stands. 

On 12 November, after 2,425 members of the Faculty Senate voted on a motion stating that the Department of Justice's indictment "is part of a broader attack on both Palestine solidarity and labor unions in the United States", results showed 58.2 percent expressed support. 

That's more than 1,000 professors, lecturers, clinicians and other University of Michigan employees. 

The Faculty Senate has nearly 8,000 members, but not all of them participate in voting.

On Wednesday, Faculty Senate chair Kentaro Toyama expressed his dismay that the University of Michigan Police Department was specifically called out in the resolution as having been party to the repression of students' speech. 

"Even if the allegations in the resolutions were true, UMPD reports to the UM President. Unless UMPD acts in defiance of UM leadership or the ethics of law enforcement, they are following civilian orders as police norms require," Toyama wrote in an email that was viewed by Middle East Eye.

The successful resolution, he added, "concerns matters that are complex and gray". 

University of Michigan still punishing pro-Palestine students after graduating
Read More »

Adi Saleem, assistant professor of Romance Languages & Literatures and Judaic Studies, introduced the resolution at the Faculty Senate's meeting earlier this month. He told MEE on Thursday that there was anti-Muslim sentiment at play, and he and another colleague were called "Nazis" afterwards by those who opposed the resolution.

"Because this resolution was moved by a Muslim professor there is obviously something antisemitic about it," he said, sarcastically.

"In the days after the resolution passed, we, the supporters of the resolution, were the focus of a right-wing and Zionist social media campaign. All of us have had our faces kind of on multiple videos accusing us of, essentially, antisemitism."

That includes assistant professor of American Culture and Digital Studies, Yarden Azoulay Katz, who told MEE that he believes the Faculty Senate chair is under both political pressure and pressure from university donors.

"Toyama's statement delivers the complete package that the university's regents, right-wing donors, and Zionist lobbying groups want to hear: that Hamas equals terrorism, that Israel has the right to exist, that Palestine is only West Bank and Gaza, and that the police keep us safe," he said.

"It also effectively says that even if the courts did not charge the defendants with vandalism or find them guilty of anything, that we know they did it and that their actions were wrong."

"It's inexcusable," he added. "Toyama has also not been upfront about the pressures being exerted on him to make such a sweeping statement."

MEE has reached out to the University of Michigan. 

Prolonged punishment

The University of Michigan has continued to discipline, fire and intimidate students and staff since the 2024 protests, many of those impacted have previously told MEE.

As recently as this June, the FBI carried out violent home raids targeting students and alumni.

But the saga began long before the Trump administration assumed power in early 2025 and vowed to crack down on pro-Palestine activists and critics of Israel. 

In September 2024, Michigan Attorney General Dana Nessel charged 11 students and alumni for what she described as "violent and criminal behaviour" in setting up the encampments. 

By May 2025, all the charges were dropped, after Nessel said the cases were just not worth her office's time anymore. 

Last month, however, the US Department of Justice, overseen by President Donald Trump's former personal lawyer, Todd Blanche, indicted 12 other students who were engaged in the 2024 anti-war protests at the University of Michigan. 

US: Lieutenant criticises police report on clearing UCLA pro-Palestine encampment
Read More »

Among the charges are "conspiracy to transmit a threat to the institution", "conspiracy to tamper with a witness", and "the destruction of property to prevent seizure". 

The US attorney for the Eastern District of Michigan, Jerome F Gorgon Jr, said the defendants "terrorize Jews". 

"The main charge against them is sending messages on the internet. Really, I mean that's what it boils down to," Katz told MEE on Thursday. "They're using conspiracy charges... without needing to have any real substantive evidence."

"The property damage that's described in the indictment, none of it concerns federal buildings, right? So, the federal government has no business even getting into a hypothetical vandalism case here," he added. 

The DOJ further alleged there was "an increased support for Hamas on college campuses" at the time of the encampments that emerged at universities across the country. 

At the time, between March and May 2024, Israel was killing up to 200 Palestinian civilians a day in its assault on Gaza, and then-President Joe Biden had refused to use any leverage to stop the attacks. 

"If you don't stand up to this right now, there's no telling how far it could escalate," a former student-turned-employee of the university, Zainab Hakim, who is named in the indictment, told MEE last year.

"They are trying to paint a peaceful expression of First Amendment rights as violent in order to repress the movement," she said. 

"I don't regret trying to do the right thing."

There is a legal fund that has been set up for the so-called "Michigan 12".

item.description:
Yemen war: How do the rival alliances and armed factions stack up?

Yemen, where civil war broke out in 2014, has recently been rocked by the worst fighting in years. A truce agreed in 2022 between the Ansar Allah, better known as the Houthis, who control the north, and forces loyal to the government in the south disintegrated when Saudi Arabia bombed Sanaa airport in July.

In August and September, the Houthis mounted a quick offensive, recapturing much of the western coast, including the port of Mocha, putting it within close range of ships passing the strategically important Bab el-Mandab strait. 

The Houthis are now targeting Aden, Yemen’s second city and seat of its internationally recognised government since the group took the capital Sanaa 12 years ago.

Meanwhile, the Houthis have tightened their decade-long siege of Taiz, blocking the road to Aden and raising the prospect of its capture.

The Saudi-backed pro-government military coalition contains a variety of armed units and local militias, each with different goals, rival leaders and origins, leading to infighting and disorganisation.

Allegiances frequently shift and evolve: the Giants Brigade and the National Resistance Forces were each previously backed by the UAE. The leaders of both, like much of the coalition, are now bankrolled by Riyadh amid its fallout with Abu Dhabi. 

With fighting spread across multiple front lines, here’s an overview of the most important military and political parties involved in the conflict.

item.description:
Gaza’s children caught in the grip of a meningitis outbreak

Submitted by Hani Abu Rezeq on Fri, 11/27/2026 - 08:11
Contaminated water, collapse of healthcare system and scarce medical supplies are fuelling a surge in infections across the besieged enclave
Nine-month-old Mohammed, who is being treated for meningitis, sits on his mother Reham Wahdan’s lap at Al-Rantisi Hospital in Gaza City (Hani Abu Rezeq/MEE)
Off

For 10 days, two-month-old Mostafa Hallawin has been bedridden at Al-Rantisi Children’s Hospital in Gaza City.

After suffering a persistent high fever, reaching 39C, and recurring abdominal swelling, the Palestinian infant was diagnosed with meningitis.

“It started with a skin rash and a high fever, with his temperature reaching 39C,” his mother, Amal, told Middle East Eye.

“Every day, doctors perform medical scans and laboratory tests,” she added, saying his condition has shown little improvement, largely because of shortages of essential medicines.

Hallawin is one of the most recent children to develop meningitis amid a spike in cases across the war-torn enclave, where Israel has all but destroyed the healthcare system and continues to ban essential medicines.

The UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (Ocha) reported 413 suspected meningitis cases in Gaza between 27 September and 31 October, including 294 viral and 119 bacterial cases. The report said 68 percent were recorded in Gaza City.

On Tuesday, the Palestinian Health Ministry declared an "epidemic alert" across Gaza, citing a sharp rise in meningitis cases and deaths.

The ministry said 1,790 people had been diagnosed with meningitis since the beginning of the year, with 15 deaths recorded. In October alone, at least 272 infections were confirmed.

The risk of infectious diseases has increased amid overcrowded displacement shelters, unsafe drinking water, damaged sanitation systems and the collapse of essential healthcare services across Gaza.

In September, the World Health Organisation (WHO) said microbiological contamination in tested water samples rose from less than six percent in January to nearly 20 percent in August.

At Al-Rantisi Children's Hospital, which was heavily damaged in Israeli attacks during the war, beds are filled with children suffering from infectious diseases, including meningitis.

The growing number of cases threatens to create conditions in which infections can spread easily between children. Amal believes her child’s condition deteriorated during his hospital stay because of overcrowding and inadequate isolation facilities.

“There is little access to basic hygiene facilities, clean food and safe drinking water,” she said.

“I appeal for medicines and essential medical equipment to be allowed into Gaza for our children.

"We have lost our homes and our lives in this war. We don’t want to lose our babies too.”

Contaminated water

For Reham Wahdan, the health crisis became personal when her nine-month-old son, Mohammed, developed a high fever.

Wahdan and her family have been living alongside other displaced families in a room in the partly destroyed Islamic University building, after their home in Shujaiya, east of Gaza City, was destroyed by an Israeli attack during the war.

She said Mohammed's health began to deteriorate a day after they visited relatives staying in a makeshift tent near their displacement shelter.

'I appeal for medicines and essential medical equipment to be allowed into Gaza for our children'

- Amal Hallawin, Palestinian mother 

She believes he got the infection from a child with meningitis whom they'd visited.

“He had suffered from a high fever for nearly a month, despite repeated attempts to give him medication to bring his temperature down,” she said. 

Wahdan took Mohammed to several medical tents and treatment points, where he was given medication to reduce his fever. His temperature would fall briefly, only to rise again.

“Doctors at Al-Rantisi Hospital performed a lumbar puncture to collect a cerebrospinal fluid sample, and the test results confirmed that he had meningitis,” she said.

Wahdan also said her family had no access to safe drinking water where they were displaced.

“We drink contaminated water, and we rely entirely on distributed food,” she said.

Deteriorating conditions

Dr Nidal Ghunaim, the deputy director-general of primary health care for public health at the Ministry of Health, said both bacterial and viral meningitis cases had increased significantly compared with previous years.

He attributed much of the rise to enterovirus, which he said was closely linked to deteriorating environmental conditions across the Gaza Strip.

The contamination of drinking water with sewage had further worsened the situation, contributing to the increase in reported infections, he said.

The situation has become even more concerning following recent heavy rainfall  in Gaza.

“Many areas were flooded with rainwater, and sewage mixed with drinking water. The destruction of infrastructure has made the situation worse, and we expect that any further wave of flooding could make things much more difficult,” he told MEE.

“There are also significant shortages of laboratory supplies, medical treatments and isolation facilities in hospitals,” Ghunaim added.

He called on the international community to intervene urgently and support a comprehensive, long-term response to Gaza's environmental and water crises.

“The extensive destruction of water infrastructure has severely affected access to safe and clean water. Restoring and rehabilitating the water network must be an essential priority,” he said.

Back at Al-Rantisi Hospital, Reem Hamada has spent the past 10 days at the bedside of her five-year-old grandson, Mohammed, after he developed a high fever.

“One day, he came back from kindergarten with a high fever. We applied cool compresses to his forehead, neck and armpits to try to bring his temperature down, but it did not improve,” she said.

Throughout the interview, Mohammed lay beside her, his eyes closed, a cool compress resting on his forehead as the fever persisted.

“He is my only grandchild. What has he done to deserve this suffering?” she said. 

“We are no longer living; we are as good as dead.”

Israel's genocide in Gaza
Ahmed Dremly

item.title: [www.middleeasteye.net] In Israel, calls for 'unity' are a code for Jewish tribal supremacy
item.description:
In Israel, calls for 'unity' are a code for Jewish tribal supremacy

Submitted by Orly Noy on Thu, 11/26/2026 - 19:43
The foundation runs deeper than a political consensus among the competing blocs: it concerns which citizens are included when they say 'we'
Former military chief Gadi Eisenkot, leader of the Yashar party, waves after national election exit polls at his party headquarters in Tel Aviv, Israel, on 28 October 2026 (Shir Torem/Reuters)
Off

The saying “when fascism comes to America, it will be wrapped in a flag and carrying a cross” is commonly attributed to American novelist and playwright Sinclair Lewis. 

German writer Thomas Mann, himself a Nobel laureate in literature, had a slightly different version: “If ever fascism should come to America, it will come in the name of freedom.” 

Former Republican President Ronald Reagan, meanwhile, offered his own version: “If fascism ever comes to America, it will come in the name of liberalism.”

Whatever form fascism may take when it arrives in the US, one thing can be said with certainty: in Israel, it arrived in the name of unity. 

It is hard to think of a word in the Hebrew language that has been more shamelessly abused than “unity” by Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s inciting, divisive gang.

Take, for example, Elisha Madan, the newly elected Likud MK who has set up a “Unity Tent” outside the Knesset. “I intend to sit in the tent day and night, in the cold and rain, to give voice to the many people who keep reaching out to me, yearning for unity,” he declared poetically. 

This great champion of unity, it is worth recalling, helped establish the settlement of Avigail. He was also filmed hurling vile slurs at the late human rights activist Ezra Nawi, who had come to the area to protect Palestinian residents from settler violence.

Common ground

Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich, the man who warned before the election that a left-wing government would pose an existential threat to the state of Israel, suddenly remembered after the vote to reach out to his “Jewish brothers” with a call for unity. 

Amir Ohana - the former Knesset speaker who boycotted the swearing-in ceremony of Supreme Court president Yitzhak Amit, and who refused to allow bereaved families into the Knesset gallery during a Netanyahu speech about the 7 October attacks, instead having them forcibly removed - also professes to see unity as a cherished goal, with the 26th Knesset holding the means to achieve it.

The use of the term 'the people of Israel' is no accident. It is a code word, an effective shortcut for establishing a shared sense of tribal belonging 

And this week, comedian Guy Hochman shoved a camera rudely into MK Ahmad Tibi’s face, shouting at him: “Ahmad, unity? Unity?” This knight of unity is the same man who found the genocide in Gaza particularly amusing, and a fitting backdrop for a stand-up performance intended to boost the morale of the forces of destruction and annihilation. 

He is also the same comedian who attended a left-wing demonstration and declared that its participants were “scarier than Qatar”. Now, he too wants unity.

It is easy to dismiss the unity tantrum gripping Netanyahu’s camp as a cynical ploy, designed to neutralise the meaning of its electoral defeat and spare its members the prospect of being banished to the opposition benches.

But the truth is that it rests on something much deeper, rooted in the anomaly of Israeli politics: a political landscape divided not primarily along ideological lines, but above all, over the question of support for Netanyahu. 

Remove Netanyahu himself from the equation, and the common ground between the two blocs is far greater than it might appear; on many issues, their areas of agreement actually outweigh their differences. 

A call for unity between two blocs that stood firmly together around the most defining event in Israel’s history since its founding - the perpetration of genocide against a besieged and defenceless Palestinian population - is not entirely baseless.

But the foundation of this call for unity runs even deeper than a consensus on any particular policy. It concerns the most instinctive sense of belonging shared by members of both blocs: who they mean when they say “we”.

Dangerous distinction

The Israeli right long ago replaced the concept of “Israeli citizens” with the tribal notion of “the people of Israel” - a term that clearly refers exclusively to the Jewish collective. This dangerous substitution is no longer confined to the right. 

“The people of Israel cannot trust Netanyahu when he claims his motives are not political … We must not allow him to exploit Israel’s security to disrupt the elections,” Yair Golan, leader of the Democrats, tweeted about a month before the election.

The distinction between “the people of Israel” and “Israeli citizens” is anything but semantic. It reflects two fundamentally different conceptions of the Israeli collective, only one of which includes Palestinian citizens of Israel. 

Why did Golan choose to invoke “the people of Israel” rather than “Israeli citizens”? Are Arab citizens of Israel not equally affected by security concerns? Do they not flee to bomb shelters - when such shelters are available to them - during wartime?

The use of the term “the people of Israel” is no accident. It is a code word, an effective shortcut for establishing a shared sense of tribal belonging and manufacturing intimacy. 

How Israel’s election is further excluding Palestinian citizens from politics
Read More »

When Yashar leader Gadi Eisenkot tells a former Likud voter, disillusioned with Netanyahu, during an election campaign that “as far as I’m concerned, there is no way the people of Israel will not prevail,” he knows exactly what he is doing: building a sense of tribal intimacy whose boundaries are perfectly clear to both men. 

It is within those boundaries that the right is now calling on him to gather under its unity campaign - boundaries that necessarily leave Arabs on the outside.

It is hardly surprising, then, that the Arab parties are the only ones presenting a civic discourse as a substantive alternative to the Jewish tribal discourse embodied in the phrase “the people of Israel”. 

Here lies one of the great paradoxes of the Zionist state. Since its founding, Israel has relentlessly sought to sever the connection between Arab citizens and their Palestinian national identity, subjecting them to a process of forced “Israelisation”.

Yet the moment Arab citizens seek to give real substance to the citizenship imposed upon them after the Nakba, “the people of Israel” are quick to reclassify them as Palestinians and push them back beyond the boundaries of the Israeli collective. This is the declared position of at least two of the four parties that make up the so-called change bloc.

The choice now facing Eisenkot is not merely between two different governing coalitions. It is a choice between two fundamentally different conceptions of the boundaries of Israeli citizenship: between “the people of Israel” and the citizens of Israel. If he chooses the former, he will become, under cover of the “unity” discourse, a pale appendage of a fully fledged Jewish-supremacist coalition. 

If he chooses the latter, he will have to accept Arab citizens as full partners in Israeli citizenship, with an equal and legitimate stake in shaping the country’s character - rather than as people whose struggle is limited to securing whatever crumbs the state is willing to throw their way.
